description_ru: Внук наследует от деда старый дом и ульи и узнаёт древний обычай: пчёлам нужно сообщить о смерти хозяина. Так начинается разговор, которого он избегал девять лет.
text:
The solicitor's letter informed Tomasz Wiśniewski that his grandfather's estate consisted of a stone cottage, a rusting Land Rover, and eleven beehives. It did not mention any money, which was a relief, since Tomasz suspected there was none, nor any instruction about what he was supposed to do with the hives, which was less of one.

He had not seen the old man in nearly nine years. There had been no dramatic quarrel, merely the slow erosion of silence, a few unanswered calls, a missed funeral, the usual small negligences by which families come apart. Now, standing at the gate of the cottage in a cold October drizzle, he felt like a man who had arrived late for an exam in a subject he had never studied.

The hives stood in a row at the bottom of the orchard, white boxes with peeling paint, each one humming at a pitch so low that he felt it in his teeth. A neighbour named Mrs Fenn, who had a face like a walnut and the manner of a retired headmistress, appeared at the hedge to inspect him.

"You'll be the grandson," she said. "He said you'd come eventually. He wasn't a man who predicted things lightly." "I don't know the first thing about bees." "Then it's as well you've got me." She sniffed. "But first you must tell them." "Tell them what?" "That he's dead, of course. It's the custom. If a beekeeper dies and nobody informs the bees, they take offence. They leave, or they sicken, or they simply stop producing. You knock on each hive three times with the house key, and you say his name, and you tell them who's in charge now."

Tomasz opened his mouth to point out that insects did not have feelings, then closed it again. Mrs Fenn had the look of a woman who had heard every objection and found them all wanting. Besides, the key was already in her outstretched hand.

So it was that, on a grey Tuesday afternoon, a thirty-four-year-old software tester found himself kneeling in wet grass and addressing a wooden box. He felt ridiculous. He knocked, three times, and cleared his throat. "Your keeper, Jan Wiśniewski, has died," he said. "I'm his grandson. I'm very sorry that I didn't come sooner."

The humming did not change, of course. Why would it? But he moved on to the second hive, and the third, and by the fifth he had stopped feeling absurd and begun to feel something else, an odd, unprotected tenderness. He found himself explaining things. That the old man had been buried beside his wife. That the funeral had been small but the soup afterwards was good. That he, Tomasz, had no idea what he was doing, but would do his best not to ruin everything.

At the ninth hive, he heard himself say the thing he had not said to anyone, including himself. "I should have come. I kept meaning to. It got harder every year, and then it was too late." A single bee crawled out onto the landing board and sat there, cleaning her antennae with great concentration. Tomasz laughed, a short, wet sound, and wiped his face with the back of his glove.

Through the winter he came every weekend. Mrs Fenn supervised from a folding chair, issuing instructions with the crispness of an air traffic controller. Under her guidance he learned that bees cluster in cold weather, shivering their flight muscles to keep the queen warm, rotating the outermost insects inward so nobody freezes for long. He learned to listen at the side of a hive, with his ear against the wood, and distinguish the contented drone of a healthy colony from the thin, anxious note of one in trouble. He found his grandfather's notebooks in a kitchen drawer, written in a cramped, slanting hand, recording dates, weather, and the temper of each colony. There were occasional digressions. Hive Six is sulking. Hive Two has opinions about the new neighbours.

In one margin, dated nine years earlier, Tomasz found a sentence that stopped him cold. T. rang today. Didn't pick up in time. Will ring back. Beneath it, in different ink, the same line appeared again on a later page, and again after that, a small stubborn refrain, as though the old man had been waiting at a telephone for years, patient as a bee in January.

He read it three times, folded the notebook shut, and went outside. The first snowdrops were showing under the apple trees. The hives were silent, as they always were in the cold, but when he laid his palm flat against the nearest one, he could feel the faintest warmth, the heartbeat of a colony that had decided to endure.

In May, the first honey came out thick and amber, tasting of blossom and rain. Tomasz put a jar on the table at Mrs Fenn's kitchen and she tasted it with her eyes closed, like a judge at a wine fair. "Not bad," she said, which from her was practically a medal. "He'd have said it was a bit thin." "He would," said Tomasz. "He'd have been right."

When she had gone, he walked down to the orchard one last time that evening and knocked on the first hive, three times, with the key. "I'm still here," he said. "I'm not going anywhere." From somewhere inside came a low hum, rising and falling, which he was perfectly willing to interpret as an answer.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: soˈlicitor, ˈnegligences, diˈgressions. Безударное «-or» и «-ences» произносите кратко: «ə».
Для «w» округлите губы и не касайтесь зубами нижней губой: wooden, winter, а не «в».
В -ing задняя часть языка касается мягкого нёба: hum-ming, без отчётливого «г» после «н».
Звук «æ» шире русского «э»: рот открыт, язык плоский: antennae, amber.

questions.question: What did Tomasz inherit?
questions.answer: A stone cottage, an old Land Rover and eleven beehives.

questions.question: What custom did Mrs Fenn insist on?
questions.answer: Telling the bees about the death by knocking on each hive three times with the key.

questions.question: What did Tomasz find in his grandfather's notebooks?
questions.answer: Notes showing that his grandfather had waited for his call and meant to ring back.

questions.question: How did the story end?
questions.answer: Tomasz promised the bees he was staying, and a hum seemed to answer.
